original_value: The goal of this case study is to demonstrate the application and utility of a developed System Dynamics (SD) model to assess the sustainability of strategic decisions for managing the wastewater collection (WWC) pipe network system for a medium-size municipality in Southern Ontario. Two asset management scenarios, suggested by the research-partnered municipality, are adapted based on the acceptable maximum fraction of pipes in the worst condition (ICG5) being equal to (1) 10% of the network-length/year, and (2) the initial 2.8% of network-length/year for the entire life cycle of the asset. The urban densification scenarios are restricted to a 50% urban densification rate. The least maximum rehabilitation rates of 1.41% and 1.85% of network length/year are found necessary to keep the ICG5 pipes fractions below the selected 10% and 2.8% thresholds, respectively. The maximum and minimum user fee-hike rates for WWC and wastewater treatment (WWT) services are adjusted to support the financial self-sustainability aspect. Results from the SD model, as presented over a 100 year simulation period, show that an accelerated rehabilitation strategy will have a lower financial cost with the lowest greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. This study highlights the implications of integrating asset management of wastewater-collection and -treatment systems. Applying such an integrated SD model will help decision makers to forecast the future trends related to social, economic, and environmental performances of wastewater infrastructure systems, and evaluate the behavior of interrelated and complex WWC and WWT systems to find synergistic cost-saving opportunities while at the same time improve sustainability.

result.paraphrase: This case study demonstrates how a developed System Dynamics (SD) model can be used to evaluate the sustainability of strategic decisions for managing the wastewater collection (WWC) pipe network of a medium-sized municipality in Southern Ontario. Based on acceptable maximum fractions of pipes in the worst condition (ICG5), two asset management scenarios proposed by the partner municipality are considered: (1) 10% of network length per year, and (2) the initial 2.8% of network length per year over the asset’s full life cycle. Urban densification scenarios are limited to a 50% densification rate. The minimum rehabilitation rates required to keep ICG5 pipe fractions below the chosen 10% and 2.8% thresholds are 1.41% and 1.85% of network length per year, respectively. To maintain financial self-sustainability, the maximum and minimum user fee-hike rates for WWC and wastewater treatment (WWT) services are adjusted. Over a 100-year simulation period, the SD model shows that an accelerated rehabilitation strategy results in lower financial cost and the lowest greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. The study underscores the value of integrating asset management for wastewater collection and treatment systems. Using such an integrated SD model can help decision makers forecast future social, economic, and environmental performance trends for wastewater infrastructure systems, and assess the dynamics of interconnected and complex WWC and WWT systems to identify synergistic cost-saving opportunities while improving sustainability.
